fact_sheet.business_description: Capital Cities is combining its broadcast and publishing operations with the national television network ABC and related media properties [D01]. The combined entity operates in media, where they sell audiences to advertisers while providing news and entertainment [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Newspapers and broadcasting: selling audiences to advertisers while supplying news/entertainment to readers/viewers [D01], [D06]
economics: Margins: Capital Cities standalone operating margins were 28.5% in 1984 [D02]. Segment margins in 1984: broadcasting 52.1%, publishing 22.5%, cable 3.3% [D06].

Capital intensity: Advertising revenue is sensitive to business conditions [D01]. Local broadcast and publishing positions are difficult to replicate, but broadcast licenses are not perpetual unregulated monopolies [D01].
Owner-earnings: FY1984 standalone: depreciation $34.084m, intangible amortization $17.633m, capital spending $53.866m; 'available cash flow' $142.734m [D02].
earnings_record: Q1 1985 net income was $27.7m vs $27.1m in 1984 (2.2% growth) [D03].
competitive_position: Established local positions are difficult to replicate [D01], [D06].
Regulatory ownership ceiling is 25% of national television homes [D06].
Network programming/local stations have different economics; strong local returns are not mechanically transferable to a network [D01].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Capital Cities standalone 1984: Cash $236.399m, Total debt $222.995m [D02].
ABC combination value is roughly $3.5 billion [D02], [D09].
Opening combined balance sheet and debt amortization schedule are not recovered [D02], [D09].
management_and_capital_allocation: Tom Murphy and Dan Burke have a long operating record [D01].
Management is noted for a low-cost, owner-oriented approach [D01].
price_and_valuation: Negotiated subscription price: $172.50 per common share for 3 million shares [D02], [D04].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Capital Cities record may not scale to the network [D05].
High acquisition prices may leave little room for disappointment [D05].
ABC earnings are subject to ratings, programming costs, advertising conditions, and competition [D05].
deal_terms_if_any: 3 million shares subscribed at $172.50 per share [D02], [D09].
berkshire_context: Berkshire has prior experience with Capital Cities and its management [D08].
A $517.5 million financing is material relative to 1984 year-end portfolio [D08].
Exact funding cash and insurance-entity allocations are not in pack [D08].
missing_data: Full opening combined balance sheet, post-deal debt amortization, normalized ABC cash-flow reconciliation, Q3 1985 results, and current market price at 1986-01-03.

understandable.evidence: The business operates in media, selling audiences to advertisers via broadcast and publishing, which are established, slow-changing areas [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: Capital Cities has demonstrated local broadcast and publishing positions that are difficult to replicate [D01], [D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Standalone EPS grew consistently from $5.38 in 1980 to $10.40 in 1984 [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: Standalone ROE remained strong between 19.5% and 21.5% from 1980-1984 with conservative debt levels [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The business generates high operating margins, specifically 28.5% standalone in 1984 [D02].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Tom Murphy and Dan Burke are well-regarded for their low-cost, owner-oriented approach [D01].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: The $3.5 billion ABC acquisition is a significant transaction that easily moves the needle for Berkshire [D02], [D08].

price_screen.evidence: While the standalone P/E is 16.59x, the complexity of the ABC integration and lack of post-deal normalized earnings make an accurate 10% earnings yield assessment difficult at this time [D02], [D04].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a collection of elite media franchises managed by exceptionally disciplined, owner-oriented operators.

gate2.why_available: The market is skeptical that the Capital Cities low-cost operating model can effectively scale to the significantly larger and more volatile ABC network environment [D05]. We disagree, as our long experience with Tom Murphy and Dan Burke provides us confidence that they will apply their same owner-oriented discipline to ABC's assets [D01], [D08]. By backing this team, we are effectively buying a wonderful business at a fair price with the expectation that management will compound value over the long term regardless of short-term network ratings fluctuations [D01].
evidence: Tom Murphy and Dan Burke are well-regarded for their low-cost, owner-oriented approach [D01].
Berkshire has prior experience with Capital Cities and its management [D08].
The combined entity operates in media with established local positions that are difficult to replicate [D01], [D06].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market fears that ABC's earnings are too dependent on unpredictable ratings, rising programming costs, and cyclical advertising conditions to maintain the high returns seen at Capital Cities [D05].
what_must_be_true: Murphy and Burke can successfully integrate ABC and impose their low-cost culture on the network operations.
The underlying demand for broadcast advertising remains durable enough to support the combined entity's returns.
The combined company's debt levels remain manageable, allowing management to focus on operations rather than financial distress.

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: 1984 standalone CapCities $10.40 EPS [D02]; combined normalized earnings not in pack

key_assumptions: Murphy/Burke operating discipline scales to ABC [D01]
Combined entity debt managed through cash flow [D02]

gate3.price_vs_value: 100% of purchase price; margin of safety provided by management track record [D01]
gate3.alternatives: Existing holdings or T-bills at 9.05% [D04]; preferred Capital Cities as it leverages proven owner-oriented management [D01]
gate3.downside_case: Overpayment for network assets resulting in stagnant growth; not a permanent loss of capital given strong station cash flows [D01]
flagged_assumptions: Combined 1986 owner earnings estimated based on 1984 standalone performance
Post-deal leverage impact on earnings assumed manageable

gate4.role_description: Berkshire's edge is patience and permanent capital, allowing us to benefit as the business compounds under the stewardship of Tom Murphy and Dan Burke [D01].
value_realisation_path: Value is realised through the superior long-term compounding of owner earnings under exceptional management [D01].
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the 1980-1999 era, our focus is on acquiring consumer franchises at fair prices and retaining ownership in excellent businesses to hold indefinitely [Instruction 5].

kill_criteria: Management loses focus on cost control or makes acquisitions outside their circle of competence [D01].
The regulatory environment shifts to cap returns or limit ownership below the thresholds required for network operation [D06].
Structural changes in the television industry render broadcast advertising significantly less effective as an audience-selling medium [D01].
gate5.berkshire_constraints: The investment must respect regulatory ownership ceilings of 25% of national television homes [D06] and be funded in a manner that preserves Berkshire's capital adequacy [D08].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Allocating capital to T-bills yielding 9.05% or existing holdings with more predictable cash flow profiles [D04].
gate5.decider_reason: The investment is a substantial, negotiated commitment in a business managed by operators I know and trust to be exceptional, fitting my 1980s era mandate for consumer franchises [D01], [Instruction 5].
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is that the unique, low-cost operating culture that generated exceptional returns at smaller, local stations cannot be successfully scaled to the far more complex and volatile national television network environment [D01], [D05].

valuation.owner_earnings: 1984 standalone $10.40 EPS; combined normalized earnings projected to grow under disciplined management
valuation.downside_case: Integration fails to yield expected cost efficiencies, resulting in stagnant growth but minimal risk of permanent capital loss due to strong cash-generating station assets

drivers.driver: We are betting on the exceptional stewardship of Tom Murphy and Dan Burke, whose disciplined, owner-oriented culture has generated superior returns for years [D01].
The business possesses a durable moat through elite local media franchises that are difficult to replicate [D01], [D06].
The acquisition of ABC transforms the entity's scale while keeping the core business understandable and within our circle of competence [D01].
We are acquiring these shares at a price that represents fair value for a wonderful business, with the expectation that management will compound value over the long term [D01].

kill_criteria: Management loses focus on cost control or makes acquisitions outside their circle of competence [D01].

Structural changes in the television industry render broadcast advertising significantly less effective as an audience-selling medium [D01].
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A departure of Tom Murphy or Dan Burke, or evidence that the network's high cost structure is undermining the company's historical operating discipline.
final.memo:
Charlie and I have long admired the operations of Capital Cities, a business that essentially functions by selling audiences to advertisers through its highly defensible broadcast and publishing assets [D01]. We understand this model well, as it relies on durable local positions that are quite difficult for competitors to replicate [D01], [D06].

The company’s record is a testament to its economics, with standalone returns on equity consistently hovering near 20% throughout the first half of the decade [D02]. While the acquisition of ABC adds complexity, the operating margins of 28.5% seen in Capital Cities' standalone business give us comfort in the underlying power of their media franchises [D02].

The true engine here is the management of Tom Murphy and Dan Burke, who are as honest and owner-oriented as any we have encountered [D01]. We are confident they will apply the same low-cost, disciplined approach to the ABC network that they have historically employed at their local stations [D01], [D08].

Many in the market fear that these operating habits will fail to scale to the larger, more volatile national network environment [D05]. We disagree, viewing this skepticism as a short-term reaction to industry ratings fluctuations rather than a reflection of long-term business value [D01].

We are paying $172.50 per share, a price we consider fair given the intrinsic value and the potential for these operators to compound capital over an indefinite horizon [D02], [D04]. While we are not looking for a quick catalyst, our expectation is that patient ownership will be rewarded as the team integrates these assets [D01].

The primary risk remains the potential inability to translate local station efficiencies to the network level, but given the station cash flows, we do not view this as a threat of permanent loss [D01]. We have sized this at 10% of our equity portfolio, reflecting our high conviction in the stewardship of Murphy and Burke [D08].
